Duration::total().nanoseconds()¶

Back to Duration API Reference

Signature¶

DurationTotal Duration::total() const;
Series DurationTotal::nanoseconds() const;

What It Does¶

Converts a Duration’s elapsed magnitude into a plain Series expressed in nanoseconds — the finest-grained unit accessor, and the one every other total() accessor is defined relative to (each just divides this value by a different constant). Useful when you need the exact underlying tick count, e.g. to inspect sign’s output, which is always exactly ±1 nanosecond in magnitude.

total() itself returns a small proxy object (DurationTotal) with one method per unit — .nanoseconds(), .microseconds(), .milliseconds(), .seconds(), .minutes(), .hours(), .days(), .weeks() — all documented together on this page and its siblings. There is no flat Duration::total_nanoseconds()/total_seconds()/etc.; total() is the sole entry point.

Parameters¶

None — both total() and nanoseconds() are zero-argument accessors.

Returns¶

DurationTotal for total() A proxy object exposing the eight unit accessors.

Series for nanoseconds() (and every other unit method on the proxy) A floating-point Series at self’s shape, in the named unit.

Examples¶

Example 1. A 90-minute Duration read as raw nanoseconds.

auto ninety_min = pluss::duration::minutes(90);
std::cout << pluss::series::print(ninety_min.total().nanoseconds());

Output¶

Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=5.4000e+12

90 minutes is 5.4 * 10^12 nanoseconds.

Notes¶

  • .total().nanoseconds() never rounds or truncates — it is the exact underlying tick count, just as a floating-point Series.

  • To go the other direction (a nanosecond count back into a Duration), use pluss::duration::nanos.

  • total() returns a proxy holding its own copy of the Duration (cheap — Duration wraps a single reference-counted Series), not a reference, so it’s safe to call directly on a temporary: pluss::duration::minutes(90).total().seconds().

  • Each unit method on the proxy computes independently on access — calling .total() itself does no conversion work; the actual "total" dispatch only runs when a specific unit method (.nanoseconds(), .hours(), etc.) is actually called.
